title: Why does red wine dry out your mouth?
body: That gripping, cotton-mouth feeling is tannin. It comes from grape skins, seeds and stems (and oak barrels). Tannins bind to proteins in your saliva, which is also why a steak makes a tannic red taste softer.
tryIt: Sip a Cabernet, then take a bite of cheese and sip again. Notice the difference?

title: "Dry" doesn't mean what you think
body: In wine, dry just means not sweet: the yeast ate almost all the sugar. A wine can taste wildly fruity (ripe cherry, mango) and still be bone dry. Fruitiness is aroma; sweetness is sugar.
tryIt: Pinch your nose while sipping. Sweetness stays, most "fruit" disappears.

title: The truth about "legs"
body: The streaks running down your glass say more about alcohol (and sugar) than quality. More alcohol means more, slower legs. They're a fun physics show (the Marangoni effect), not a score.
tryIt: Compare the legs of a 12% white and a 15% Zinfandel.

title: Most reds are served too warm
body: "Room temperature" dates from cold European cellars. A big red shines around 16 to 18°C (60 to 65°F). Too warm and it tastes boozy and flat. Fifteen minutes in the fridge fixes it.
tryIt: Chill half a glass of red briefly and taste it next to the other half.

title: Acidity is the secret to food pairing
body: Acidity makes your mouth water. High-acid wines (Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Barbera, Champagne) cut through fat and salt and refresh your palate, which is why they're the most food-friendly wines on earth.
tryIt: Try a crisp white with fried food or anything with a squeeze of lemon.

title: Why swirl?
body: Swirling pulls oxygen into the wine and lifts aromatic compounds out of it. Since most of what we call "taste" is actually smell, a good swirl can double what you notice.
tryIt: Smell a wine before swirling, then after. Count the new smells.

title: Where vanilla in wine comes from
body: Vanilla, toast, coconut and baking-spice notes usually come from oak barrels, not grapes. American oak leans coconut and dill; French oak leans vanilla and spice. New barrels give more flavor than old ones.
tryIt: Compare an unoaked Chablis with an oaky California Chardonnay.

title: What a vintage year actually tells you
body: The vintage is the year the grapes were picked. In cool, fickle places (Burgundy, Germany, Champagne) weather swings make a big difference year to year. In sunny, steady regions it matters much less.
tryIt: Next time you shop, check whether the label has a year at all. Most Champagne doesn't.

title: Old World vs New World, in one line
body: Old World (Europe) labels usually name the place (Chablis, Rioja, Barolo); New World labels usually name the grape (Chardonnay, Tempranillo, Nebbiolo). Same grapes, different way of thinking.
tryIt: Chablis is 100% Chardonnay. Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc. Barolo is Nebbiolo.

title: Terroir: wine's sense of place
body: Terroir is the French idea that soil, slope, climate and local tradition all leave a fingerprint on a wine. It's why the same grape tastes different in Oregon, Burgundy and New Zealand.
tryIt: Taste two Pinot Noirs from different countries side by side.

title: How rosé gets its color
body: Almost all rosé is made from red grapes whose skins touch the juice for just a few hours. The color comes from the skins, so a short soak gives pink instead of red. Blending red and white is rare (Champagne is the famous exception).
tryIt: Look for a Provence rosé: pale, dry and made this way.

title: Where Champagne bubbles come from
body: In the traditional method, a still wine gets a dose of sugar and yeast, then is sealed in its bottle. The second fermentation creates CO2 that can't escape, so it dissolves into the wine. Pop the cork and it rushes out as bubbles.
tryIt: Cava and Crémant use the same method as Champagne, often for a third of the price.

title: Do you really need to decant?
body: Decanting does two jobs: it separates old wines from their sediment, and it gives tight young reds air to open up. Most everyday wines don't need it, but a young Barolo or Cabernet often tastes better after an hour.
tryIt: Pour a young red into a big jug for 30 minutes and compare it with a fresh pour.

title: Light, medium, full: what "body" means
body: Body is how heavy a wine feels in your mouth, like skim milk vs whole milk vs cream. More alcohol, sugar and extract mean fuller body. Pinot Noir is light; Cabernet and Syrah are full.
tryIt: Swish a sip of water, then a sip of wine. Feel the weight.

title: Screw caps aren't a sign of cheap wine
body: Much of the wine from New Zealand and Australia, including excellent bottles, is sealed with screw caps. They keep fresh aromas locked in and avoid cork taint, a musty fault that ruins a small share of corked bottles.
tryIt: A wine that smells like wet cardboard or a damp basement is probably "corked". You can return it.

title: The sulfite headache myth
body: Sulfites are added to almost all wine as a preservative, but white wine and dried fruit often contain more than red. Headaches are more often down to alcohol, dehydration or histamines. Drink a glass of water with every glass of wine.
tryIt: Alternate wine and water at your next dinner and notice how you feel the next day.

title: What "old vines" means
body: Older vines produce fewer grapes, but they're often more concentrated. There's no legal definition in most places, so "old vines" (vieilles vignes) can mean 30 years or 100. Some Zinfandel and Grenache vines are well over a century old.
tryIt: Look for "old vine" on a Zinfandel label and compare it with a regular one.

title: The one pairing rule that always works
body: Match weight with weight. Delicate food likes delicate wine; rich food likes rich wine. Then go further: what grows together goes together. Tomato sauce and Chianti, goat cheese and Sancerre, paella and Rioja.
tryIt: Pick tonight's wine from the same region as tonight's dish.

title: Spicy food? Reach for a little sweetness
body: High alcohol makes chili burn hotter. A slightly sweet, low-alcohol white like off-dry Riesling or Gewürztraminer cools the heat and loves Thai, Indian and Sichuan food.
tryIt: Try a German Kabinett Riesling with your next curry.

title: Does the glass really matter?
body: Shape matters more than price. A bowl that narrows at the top traps aromas so your nose gets more. One good all-purpose glass beats a cabinet of specialist ones.
tryIt: Smell the same wine from a tumbler and from a wine glass.

title: How long does an open bottle last?
body: Recork it and keep it in the fridge (reds too). Most still wines stay good for 2 to 4 days; fortified wines like Port for weeks. Bubbles last a day or two with a stopper.
tryIt: Taste a red on day one and again on day two. Some get better.

title: What is natural wine?
body: Natural wine has no strict legal definition, but it usually means organic grapes, wild yeasts, nothing added or removed, and little or no sulfur. Results range from vibrant to funky. It's a style, not a guarantee of quality.
tryIt: Ask a wine bar for a natural wine "that's clean, not funky" to start gently.

title: Your nose does most of the tasting
body: Your tongue picks up sweet, sour, salty, bitter and savory. Everything else (cherry, leather, violets, smoke) is smell, picked up both through your nose and from the back of your mouth.
tryIt: Name three smells before your first sip, even if you feel silly.

title: Where the value is
body: Famous names cost more. The best value usually comes from famous grapes in less famous places: Portuguese reds, Spanish Garnacha, Chilean Carménère, South African Chenin Blanc, Loire Cabernet Franc.
tryIt: Swap your usual bottle for one from a country you've never tried.

title: Port, Sherry and Madeira in one breath
body: Fortified wines get a shot of grape spirit. Add it during fermentation and the wine stays sweet (Port). Add it after, and it can be dry (most Sherry). Madeira is deliberately heated, which makes it almost indestructible.
tryIt: A chilled dry Fino Sherry with salted almonds is a classic for a reason.

title: Three things every label tells you
body: Look for the producer (who made it), the place (where the grapes grew) and the vintage (when they were picked). The grape may or may not be listed. Everything else is extra information or marketing.
tryIt: Pick a bottle at home and find those three things.

title: Cool climate vs warm climate
body: Cool regions give wines with higher acidity, lower alcohol and tart fruit (cranberry, green apple). Warm regions give riper, rounder wines with jammy fruit (blackberry jam, pineapple). Same grape, different personality.
tryIt: Compare a Chardonnay from Chablis with one from California.

title: How to order wine at a restaurant without fear
body: Tell the server three things: red or white, a flavor you like ("juicy", "crisp", "earthy"), and a price by pointing at it on the list. Good staff love this. The second-cheapest bottle is rarely the best value.
tryIt: Next time, say "Something like this, around this price" and point.
